documents.title: Pediatric Hypertension Guideline

chunks.content: Background Over the past 20 years, there has been a secular escalating tendency of childhood hypertension (HTN). Song et al. in their systematic review and meta-analysis of 47 articles to estimate the global prevalence of pediatric HTN noticed a gradual rising trend of 75%-79% between 2000 and 2015. The prevalence of childhood HTN was lowest in the 1990s (1.26%), modest in the 2000s (3.3%), and peaked in the period of 2010–2014 (6.02%) [ ]. In line with Song analysis, Crouch et al. in their systematic review and meta-analysis of 41 articles from African countries among children aged 3–19 years deduced duplication of the estimated pooled prevalence of pediatric HTN after 2015 (10%) compared to before 2015 (5.6%) [ ]. The global meta-analysis of childhood BP profile is alarming; it revealed an overall elevated BP and HTN prevalence of 9.67% and 4% respectively with the highest HTN prevalence in the African and Eastern Mediterranean Regions (6.94% and 5.26% respectively) [ ]. The meta-analysis of BP among African children yielded an overall elevated BP and HTN prevalence of 11.38% and 7.45% respectively [ ]. Unlike adults, the blood pressure (BP) status in children and adolescents (1–18 years) is assessed against the normative distribution of BP in healthy children after adjustment to the child sex, age, and height. Several childhood BP distribution norms have been developed. The most recent of which has been developed by the American Academy of Pediatrics (AAP) in the clinical practice guidelines for screening of the childhood BP in 2017 [ ]. The BP profile in children and adolescents is staged as normal, elevated BP, stage 1, or stage 2 HTN based on readings and classification according to the percentiles. Childhood HTN is considered when the systolic BP (SBP) and/ or diastolic BP (DBP) readings are ≥ 95th percentile on at least 3 separate occasions [ ]. Clinically, high BP in childhood is often asymptomatic and discovered incidentally. The signs and symptoms commonly associated with high BP are headache, vomiting, chest pain, palpitation, shortness of breath, and seizures [ ]. Persistence of elevated BP and development of HTN in childhood dramatically damage the blood vessels of the vital organs and prematurely develop long-term complications of the cardiovascular system (left ventricular hypertrophy, coronary artery diseases and strokes), eyes, and kidneys [ , ]. High BP in younger children is usually secondary to an underlying cause. By time, older children, like adults, are more likely to have primary HTN associated with the same unmodifiable (age, sex, family history, and ethnicity) and modifiable (excess weight, smoking, unhealthy diets, and physical inactivity) risk factors [ ]. Obesity has been shown to be the most paramount risk factor for elevated BP during childhood. Several studies have endorsed the strong association between body mass index (BMI) and elevated BP in childhood worldwide [ , ]. Moreover, childhood BP could be affected by different dietary habits like unhealthy high intake of saturated/trans fats, free sugars, and sodium with low consumption of fruits and vegetables [ ]. In addition, strong positive correlation was revealed between sedentary behaviors and high BP levels [ ]. Undetected high childhood BP is so common. Factors contributing to such under-recognition are unawareness of childhood high BP and its significance, work overflow, no measurement of child BP, poor staff training, complexity of the diagnostic technique, need for repeated visits for confirmation, misinterpretation of BP readings, and poor perception of primary HTN and its effects in children [ , ]. Elevated BP in childhood is an unseen source of HTN in adulthood. BP tracking from childhood through adulthood has shown an eminent correlation between higher BP in childhood through adulthood with onset of HTN in early adulthood [ ]. Methods The current study aimed to estimate the prevalence of high BP (elevated BP and HTN) among preparatory schoolchildren in El-Beheira Governorate, Egypt and to identify correlates associated with high BP. A cross-sectional study was conducted in 4 randomly selected governmental preparatory schools in Damanhur district of El Behera Governorate, Egypt. From a previous study, the prevalence of high BP among schoolchildren was 9.7% [ ]. Using margin of error of 2.5%, design effect of 1.5, and confidence level of 95%, the minimum required sample size was 807 students. The sample size was calculated using Epi-info software. The current study included apparently healthy preparatory schoolchildren aged 11–14 years at the selected schools to be eligible and could participate in the study with the exclusion of schoolchildren who had chronic debilitating diseases or did not provide their parent / legal guardian informed consent. Sampling approach was adopted using multistage random sampling technique. At first, Damanhur was selected among the 15 districts of El-Behera governorate using simple random sampling (SRS). size was 807 students. The sample size was calculated using Epi-info software. The current study included apparently healthy preparatory schoolchildren aged 11–14 years at the selected schools to be eligible and could participate in the study with the exclusion of schoolchildren who had chronic debilitating diseases or did not provide their parent / legal guardian informed consent. Sampling approach was adopted using multistage random sampling technique. At first, Damanhur was selected among the 15 districts of El-Behera governorate using simple random sampling (SRS). Then, for geographic representation, Damanhur district was subdivided geographically into four semi-equal divisions (A, B, C, & D). Using SRS, the first division was selected and titled A and assigned randomly for the selection of a girls’ preparatory school. Divisions B, C, and D were alternatively assigned to boys, girls, and boys’ preparatory schools. Then, a list of all public boys’ preparatory schools (division B and D) and girls’ preparatory schools (division A and C) was prepared for each division. From the prepared list, four preparatory schools were randomly selected (one from each prepared list): two girls’ schools from divisions A and C and two boys’ schools from divisions B and D. At each school, a list of all classes for each grade was prepared. Then, 6 classes were randomly selected (2 classes per grade) using SRS. Finally, within each class, all eligible children were included in the study. A total of 912 students were initially invited to participate in the study from the selected schools. Of them, 856 students actually participated in the current study with 93.9% response rate while the other 38 students were absent while conducting the current study or did not provide their parent / legal guardian informed consent. All participants were interviewed for filling a pre-designed, structured questionnaire (Supplementary file 1) including the following: (a) Socio-demographic data: age, sex, class grade, parents’ level of education. (b) Personal habits of cigarettes smoking and physical activity frequency. (c) Dietary habits: adding table salt and ten questions were posted to inquire about the frequency of different food items. Except for adding table salt question, the frequency of the ten different food items [1- vegetables, 2- fruits, 3- salted food, 4- ketchup, mayonnaise, or other sauces, 5- processed meat, 6- fried food, 7- fast food, 8- chocolate and biscuits, 9- soft drinks, and 10- canned juices] was categorized as follows: never, once monthly, once weekly, 2–3 times weekly, and daily. The frequencies of never, once monthly, and once weekly were scored 1 for intake of vegetables and fruits. While the frequencies of 2–3 times weekly and daily were scored 0. Conversely the frequency of other remaining food items including were scored as 0 for never, once monthly, once weekly and 1 for 2–3 times weekly and daily. Scores of 0 and 1 indicate low risk and high risk respectively. The total score of the ten questions ranged from 0 to 10. A cutoff point of 5 was arbitrarily chosen to determine the level of dietary risk as follows: <5: low risk and ≥ 5 high risk. This was an exploratory risk score used to provide a composite indicator of overall dietary risk. The selection and development of the risk score was done by a panel of three experts in public health and nutrition based on different dietary habits that could affect childhood BP status [ , ]. (d) Family history of chronic diseases: HTN, cardiac diseases, diabetes mellitus (DM), and obesity. Then the following measurements were obtained: (a) Anthropometric measurements: weight in kilogram (kg), height in centimeter (cm), and waist circumference (cm) were measured according to the procedures described by Gibson 2023 [ ]. BMI was calculated as weight (kg) to height in meter (m) square (kg/ m 2 ). Evaluation of BMI based on the score of centile was interpreted as follows: underweight: BMI for age below 5th centile, normal: BMI for age from above or equal to 5th centile to below 85th centile, overweight: BMI for age equal to or above 85th centile but less than 95th centile, and obese: BMI for age equal to or above 95th centile [ ]. Waist (cm) to height (cm) ratio was calculated. A cutoff of 0.5 was used to define abdominal obesity for both sexes [ ]. (b) Auscultatory BP measurement: using a mercury sphygmomanometer (KBM, model number SM-300, Kawamoto corporation, Osaka, Japan), in the seated position with supported back, exposed right arm, with at least a 10-min rest period prior to its measurement, and using appropriate cuff bladder length (≥ 80–100%) of the child’s upper arm circumference. Three measurements were taken for each participant with 2-minute interval, and the average was recorded. Students with high BP readings (elevated BP, stage 1 HTN & stage 2 HTN) were rechecked three times on 3 consecutive days to confirm

used to define abdominal obesity for both sexes [ ]. (b) Auscultatory BP measurement: using a mercury sphygmomanometer (KBM, model number SM-300, Kawamoto corporation, Osaka, Japan), in the seated position with supported back, exposed right arm, with at least a 10-min rest period prior to its measurement, and using appropriate cuff bladder length (≥ 80–100%) of the child’s upper arm circumference. Three measurements were taken for each participant with 2-minute interval, and the average was recorded. Students with high BP readings (elevated BP, stage 1 HTN & stage 2 HTN) were rechecked three times on 3 consecutive days to confirm the diagnosis for those with sustained high readings over 3 visits [ ]. Prior to launching the study, researchers measured BP for 20 children, who were not included in the current study, to ensure validity, agreement, quality, and standardization. BP of the studied students was classified according to the new American normative BP in healthy children and adolescents as follows: Children aged 1–13 years: Normal BP: <90th percentile, elevated BP: ≥90th - <95th percentile or 120/80 mm Hg - <95th percentile (whichever was lower), stage 1 HTN: ≥95th - <95th percentile + 12 mm Hg or 130/80–139/89 mm Hg (whichever was lower), and stage 2 HTN: ≥95th percentile + 12 mm Hg or ≥ 140/90 mm Hg (whichever was lower). Children aged > 13 years: Normal BP: <120/<80 mmHg, elevated BP: 120/<80 mmHg − 129/<80 mm Hg, stage 1 HTN: 130/ 80–139/ 89 mm Hg, and stage 2 HTN: ≥140/90 mm Hg [ ]. All participants with stage 2 HTN were immediately referred for medical consultation. Statistical analysis Collected data were coded, revised, cleaned, tabulated, and analyzed through IBM SPSS Statistics version 27 using the appropriate descriptive and analytical statistics. The descriptive statistics included the percentages (%), arithmetic mean (X̅), and standard deviation (SD) which described various qualitative and quantitative data of the study participants. The analytical statistics entailed the Chi squared test (χ 2 ), student t test, and analysis of variance (ANOVA). All the studied variables were included in the univariate analysis while the multivariate logistic regression analysis was conducted for variables with p value < 0.1 to determine predictors for having high BP. Multicollinearity among all the independent variables included in the multivariate logistic regression was assessed through variance inflation factor (VIF) to ensure the validity of the regression model. All VIF values were < 2.0 (ranged from 1.024 to 1.775) indicating no evidence of multicollinearity. The statistical fitness of the multivariate logistic regression model was assessed using the Omnibus Test of Model Coefficients. The model was statistically significant, χ 2 = 318.36, p < 0.05. The proportion of variance explained by the predictors was estimated using Cox & Snell and Nagelkerke R 2 statistics. This revealed that the model explained 31.1% (Cox & Snell R 2 ) to 53.1% (Nagelkerke R 2 ) of the variance in BP status and correctly classified 88.9% of cases. Also, the Hosmer and Lemeshow test was applied to assess the goodness of fit, where a non-significant result ( p > 0.05) indicated that model adequately fit the data and suggested good alignment between predictors and outcome. In all applied analytical statistical tests, p value ≤ 0.05 was considered significant. Results A sum of 856 students equally distributed (50%) among boys and girls, of an average age of 13.3 ± 0.66 years took part in the study. Nearly half of their fathers and mothers completed secondary school education. 59%, 27%, and 14% of them practiced physical activity daily, 2–3 times/ week, and ≤ 1 time/ week, respectively. 40.4% of students reported adding table salt while eating. Based on the developed dietary risk scale, 28.9% were classified having high risk. Family history of HTN was reported by 20.1% of the students [Table ]. Table demonstrated the students’ anthropometric data. These latter recorded an average of 76.78 ± 9.78 cm for waist circumference, 20.6 ± 4.42 kg/m2 BMI, and 0.48 ± 0.06 for waist to height ratio with significant higher averages among girls than boys, ( p < 0.001). The BMI status frequency was mostly headed by normal weight (68.3%) followed by obese (13.6%) and overweight (13%). Only 34.2% of the students were diagnosed with abdominal obesity. Girls had higher frequency of Obesity (15.3% vs. 11.7%), overweight (15.8% vs. 10.1%) and abdominal obesity (40.5% vs. 27.9%) than boys, ( p < 0.001). Table ; Fig. displayed the students’ BP status according to the new American normative BP in healthy children and adolescents. At the first reading, 78.4%, 4.4%, and 17.2% of students were respectively classified to have normal BP, elevated BP and HTN. At the third reading, the corresponding values changed to 84%, 9.1%, and 6.9% respectively. At the first reading, 78.4%, 4.4%, and 17.2% of students were respectively classified to have normal BP, elevated BP and HTN. At the third reading, the corresponding values changed to 84%, 9.1%, and 6.9% respectively. In Table , among the socio-demographic characteristics, only age and sex owed significant relationship to BP. The average age of the students studied was 13.27 ± 0.66 years for normal BP group, 13.49 ± 0.62 elevated BP group, and 13.46 ± 0.6 for hypertensive group with overall significant difference, p = 0.004. Moreover, salient higher frequency of HTN (10%) and elevated BP (12.6%) among girls in comparison to boys (3.8% & 5.6%) was evident, p < 0.001. There was a significant higher frequency of HTN and elevated BP among students practicing physical activity ≤ once a week (17.5% & 25%) than those practicing physical activity 2–3 times a week (14.7% & 17.3%) and daily (0.8% & 1.6%), ( p < 0.001). Further, there was a significant higher frequency of HTN and elevated BP among students classified as having high-risk diet (15% & 16.6%) and those used added table salt (15.6% & 18.5%) compared to those classified as having low risk diet (3.6% & 6.1%) and those did not use added table salt (1% & 2.7%), p < 0.001. The recall revealed that the only significant linkage of positive HTN family history was to each of HTN (HTN: 12.8% vs. 5.4%) and elevated BP (11.6% vs. 8.5); χ 2 = 14.172 ( p < 0.001). Waist circumference, BMI, and waist to height ratio were the highest among students with HTN (87.66 ± 11.5 cm, 25.92 ± 5.72 kg/m 2 , & 0.54 ± 0.07), followed by those with elevated BP (84.32 ± 10.64 cm, 24.14 ± 4.84 kg/m 2 , & 0.52 ± 0.06), and lowest with those with normal BP (75.07 ± 8.5 cm, 19.78 ± 3.7 kg/m 2 , & 0.47 ± 0.05) and the differences in-between was statistically significant, p < 0.001. In exact terms, the frequency of HTN and elevated BP was significantly higher among obese children (24.1% & 21.6%) and overweight children (9.9% & 21.6%) compared to normal weight ones (3.4% & 5.6%), p < 0.001. Furthermore, the frequency of HTN and elevated BP was significantly higher among children with abdominal obesity (13.7% & 15.4%) compared to those without (3.4% & 5.9%), p < 0.001. Univariate analysis of variables showed prominent association between high BP and age (crude odds ratio (COR) = 1.651, 95% confidence interval (CI); 1.233–2.229), girls (COR = 2.811, 95% CI; 1.891–4.178), third school grade (COR = 1.742, 95% CI; 1.109–2.738), physically activity ≤ once weekly (COR = 30.366, 95% CI; 15.424–59.785) & 2–3 times weekly physical activity (COR = 19.364, 95% CI; 10.253–36.571), high risk diet (COR = 4.302, 95% CI; 2.944–6.289), usage of added table salt (COR = 13.374, 95% CI; 8.037–22.257), positive family history of HTN (COR = 2.003, 95% CI; 1.330–3.018), and being overweight (COR = 3.718, 95% CI; 2.243–6.161) and obese (COR = 8.444, 95% CI; 5.322–13.399), and abdominal obesity (COR = 4.016, 95% CI; 2.744–5.877), (p < 0.05). While the multivariate analysis including the abovementioned variables revealed that physically activity ≤ once weekly (adjusted odds ratio (AOR) = 15.679, 95% CI; 6.936–35.443) & 2–3 times weekly physical activity (AOR = 10.738, 95% CI; 5.247–21.973), usage of added table salt (AOR = 5.745, 95% CI; 3.108–10.617), being overweight (AOR = 2.735, 95% CI; 1.298–5.765) and obese (AOR = 7.463, 95% CI; 3.414–16.314) were the predictors for having high BP level among the students, ( p < 0.05) [Table ]. Discussion The analysis of Song et al. revealed an overall 4% global pooled prevalence of pediatric HTN with higher prevalence in low- and middle-income countries (LMICs) compared to high-income countries (HIC). Also, the highest HTN prevalence was noticed in the African (6.94%) and East Mediterranean Regions (5.26%) [ ]. The pooled prevalence of pediatric HTN among African children was almost doubled (7.45%) according to Crouch et al. [ ] Country wise, the prevalence of pediatric HTN was quite variable. It was almost 6% in Iran, China, and India [ – ]. Slightly higher prevalence of pediatric HTN (8%) was reported in Egypt and India [ , ]. Further increased prevalence of pediatric HTN was noticed in Tanzania (10.8%), Jazan, Saudi Arabia (11.6%), and in India (12.4%) [ – ]. A much higher prevalence of pediatric HTN was recorded in Turkey (14.8%), Jeddah University Hospital, Saudi Arabia (15.2%), and in Tunisia (15.4%) [ – ]. An

An Extremely higher prevalence of pediatric HTN was reported in India (19.7% and 23%) [ , ]. On the contrary, low prevalence of pediatric HTN was noted in cross-sectional studies in Cameron (1.6%) and in India (2.7%) [ , ]. In line with Ebrahimi et al. [ ], Lu et al. [ ], and Patel et al. [ ], the current study yielded a prevalence of childhood HTN of 6.9% among the studied students. Similar to pediatric HTN, elevated pediatric BP prevalence varied country wise. It was lowest in India (3.2%) [ ] and Tanzania (4.4%) [ ], modest in Jeddah, Saudi Arabia (6%) [ ], China (6.6%) [ ], India (6.9%) [ ], Iran (7.4%) [ ], and in Cameron (8.1%) [ ], and highest in Turkey (11.2%) [ ], Jazan, Saudi Arabia (12%) [ ], , Tunisia (12.4%) [ ], India (13.4%) [ ], and in Egypt (14.7%) [ ]. An extremely higher prevalence of elevated pediatric BP (21.6%) was seen in India [ ]. In line with Song et al. [ ], Crouch et al. [ ], Ebrahimi et al. [ ], Chelo et al. [ ], Çam and Ustuner [ ], El-Setouhy et al. [ ], , and Soua et al. [ ], the current study revealed a prevalence of elevated pediatric BP of 9.1% among the studied students. The discrepancy in the prevalence of pediatric HTN and elevated BP could be explained on the basis of variation in the research approach, procedures, and confounders. The influence of adherence to the standardized three separate readings technique of BP measurement for the diagnosis of pediatric HTN was evident. As it helps a lot to achieve accurate diagnosis of pediatric HTN, avoid white coat HTN, and avert other conditions such as child activity and emotional state and the surrounding circumstances that might interfere with BP measurement [ ]. Although BP was measured on three consecutive days, the prevalence of HTN dropped by approximately 60% from 17.2% on the first reading to 11.8% on the second reading and reached 6.9% on the third reading. The significance of adherence to the three readings of childhood BP to diagnose HTN was quite evident in Sun et al. systematic review and meta-analysis of 21 studies including 179,561 children [ ]. Similar findings were endorsed by Marcovecchio et al. and Zhang et al. in their cross-sectional studies [ , ]. Deviation from the standardized 3-reading protocol for BP measurement could be the main contributor to the extreme high prevalence of pediatric HTN in the studies of Das et al. [ ] who considered HTN based on the mean of 3 BP readings in the same visit and Narang et al. [ ] who diagnosed HTN based on only 2 readings in the same visit separated by 5-minute interval. The role of other confounding factors shared the responsibility for the discrepancy of pediatric HTN prevalence. The influence of age of the study participants was well obvious. Inclusion of younger children diluted the prevalence of pediatric HTN [ , ], while the inclusion of older children cumulated it [ – ]. The impact of the study settings on childhood HTN prevalence was evident by Ghamri et al. who conducted their study at health facility in Jaddah [ ]. Age is a major contributor to development and progression of HTN. Compared to younger children, older ones had higher HTN and elevated BP prevalence [ ]. Again, age correlated positively with both SBP and DBP among children [ ]. Also, children with high BP possessed statistically significantly higher average age than normal BP [ , ]. In congruence with the previous studies, the current study showed higher average age among elevated BP children and hypertensive children compared to normotensive ones. The impact of sex on childhood HTN and elevated BP was obvious. Prominent higher frequency of HTN and elevated BP in girls in comparison to boys was evident in the current study. Salient prevalence of elevated BP and HTN among girls in comparison to boys was well evident in Crouch et al. meta-analysis [ ], and cross-sectional studies in Saudi Arabia [ , ], India [ , , ], and in Iran [ ]. The impact of sex on childhood HTN and elevated BP was obvious. Prominent higher frequency of HTN and elevated BP in girls in comparison to boys was evident in the current study. Salient prevalence of elevated BP and HTN among girls in comparison to boys was well evident in Crouch et al. meta-analysis [ ], and cross-sectional studies in Saudi Arabia [ , ], India [ , , ], and in Iran [ ]. Conversely, higher prevalences of pediatric HTN and elevated BP were documented among boys than girls in Egypt and Tunisia [ , ]. The higher frequency of childhood HTN among girls than boys logically coincided with the higher frequency of adulthood HTN among women than men in Egypt as mentioned in the World Health Organization (WHO) 2023 Report and Fares and Soliman cross-sectional study [ , ]. Besides, it was evident in the current study that girls had significantly higher frequency of obesity, overweight and abdominal obesity than boys. Hypertension often occurs in familial clusters and seems to be heritable. Remarkable inclination of both childhood HTN and elevated BP towards positive family than the negative one was well seen in the current study. Concomitant to the current results, solid connection between childhood HTN and elevated BP and positive family history was noted in Egypt [ ], Saudi Arabia [ , ], and in India [ ]. Physical inactivity is an eminent modifiable risk factor for HTN. Compared to physically active children, inactive ones showed higher prevalence of HTN and elevated BP in Egypt and China [ , ]. Concomitantly, the current study ascertained this relationship. The contribution of dietary habits to development of childhood HTN has been widely studied worldwide. A significant observational connection between consumption of foods poor in vegetables and fruits and rich in fried salty proteins to HTN was exhibited [ , ]. In the same context, the current study found significantly higher frequency of HTN and elevated BP among students classified as high-risk diet and those used added table salt compared to those classified as low risk diet and those did not use added table salt. Worldwide, the sacred union between obesity / overweight and high BP readings has been strongly affirmed. Higher prevalence of elevated BP and HTN among obese / overweight children than normal weight ones was inferred in Africa [ ], Egypt [ ], Saudi Arabia [ ], Tunisia [ ], India [ , ], and in Tanzania [ ]. Likewise, the frequency of elevated BP and HTN was highest, modest, and lowest among obese, overweight, and normal weight children respectively in different studies [ , , , , ]. Additionally, higher prevalence of elevated BP and HTN was noted among children with abdominal obesity than non-obese ones [ , ]. The SBP and DBP readings positively correlated with each of waist circumference and waist to height ratio in India [ ]. Moreover, hypertensive Chinese children owed higher average waist circumference and waist to height ratio in comparison to those with normal BP [ , ]. In congruence, the current study affirmed this prominent association. The multivariate analysis accredited the predictivity of different correlates worldwide. It attested the predictivity of high waist circumference, overweight and obesity, family history of HTN, lack of regular physical activity, and increasing age were the significant predictors for childhood HTN in Egypt; [ ] obesity and overweight in Saudi Arabia [ ], and overweight/ obesity and family history of HTN in Saudi Arabi [ ], obesity and overweight in Turkey [ ], and overweight/obesity and high consumption of salted food in India [ ]. In concordance with the previous studies, the multivariate analysis in the current study confirmed the predictivity of physically activity ≤ once weekly & 2–3 times weekly physical activity, usage of added table salt, being overweight and obese for having high BP level among the students. The consistency of obesity and overweight predictivity in the current and previous studies could be ascribed to the dependence on the actual objective anthropometric measurements (weight, height, and waist circumference) unlike the subjective family history, physical activity, and dietary habits data that relied on the recall. The study had a limitation of cross-sectional design adoption which cannot establish a definitive causal link between risk factors and high BP; however, this is strongly mitigated by the solid and rigorous methodology employed. Despite following the AAP 2017 guidelines for BP status classification, BP measurements were done over three consecutive days for confirmation rather than the application of measurement over three separate occasions. The study had a limitation of cross-sectional design adoption which cannot establish a definitive causal link between risk factors and high BP; however, this is strongly mitigated by the solid and rigorous methodology employed. Despite following the AAP 2017 guidelines for BP status classification, BP measurements were done over three consecutive days for confirmation rather than the application of measurement over three separate occasions. Additionally, dietary intake and physical activity were self-reported that might introduce measurement limitation because of the recall bias. However, data were collected through interviewing questionnaire instead of the self-administered questionnaire to ensure response and quality of the data. The current study also ascertained the association between HTN and studied variables that might need further longitudinal follow up studies to establish this causality. Moreover, the study restricted to only one Egyptian Governorate. To be generalizable to the overall Egyptian situation, the study needs to be replicated to represent all Egyptian Governorates. However, this is offset by the large and representative sample size of 856 students. The use of a multi-stage random sampling technique and a sample size that exceeded the statistical requirement ensured that the data is highly reliable and provided a precise reflection of the pediatric population, offering a strong foundation for future national-scale research. Conclusions Screening of schoolchildren has explicitly unveiled the high frequency of high BP of elevated BP and HTN among preparatory schoolchildren. Strikingly, age, female sex, family history of HTN, physical inactivity, bad dietary habits, overweight, obesity, and abdominal obesity correlated robustly with childhood elevated BP and HTN. These associations emphasized the importance of lifestyle modification in rectifying childhood high BP levels. Pursuant to the current study, it is critical to apply preventive strategies that emphasize awareness, screening, and early detection of childhood elevated BP and HTN. This can be achieved through the conduction of a nationwide multicenter cross-sectional study for early detection of childhood elevated BP and HTN and development of an Egyptian childhood normative BP profile. Besides, further longitudinal prospective cohort studies are needed to track children over time to establish causality of the identified associated factors of high BP. documents.title: Pediatric Obesity Treatment

chunks.content: Introduction The prevalence of type 2 diabetes (T2D) in adolescents is steadily increasing specifically among historically marginalized communities. Compared to adults, youth-onset T2D has a more aggressive disease phenotype, leading to earlier development of complications. , Therefore, there is a need to identify therapies that protect and restore functioning β-cells early in diagnosis and can be widely implemented across settings. Little is known about the efficacy of non-pharmacological, dietary interventions targeting β-cell function and body fat mass in adolescents with T2D. , Adherence to comprehensive lifestyle interventions is challenging for adolescents, in part because these approaches require frequent monitoring and engaging in multiple behavioral changes continuously. Therefore, there is a growing interest in simplifying intervention recommendations to decrease reliance on numeracy, goal-setting, and complex skillsets. – One simpler and promising approach is based on timing of eating. Time-restricted eating (TRE) is a dietary approach that involves shortening the eating window to a pre-specified number of hours per day and fasting for the remaining hours of the day without necessarily altering diet quality and quantity. Preliminary evidence in adults, has shown that compared to the average eating window of 12 to 14 hours, TRE reduces body weight and fat mass, improves insulin sensitivity, reduces hepatic fat accumulation, and is safe with no negative effect on daily functionning. – Specifically in individuals with T2D, increasing daily fasting duration minimizes glycemic excursions and leads to reduction in endogenous glucose production (both of which will reduce insulin secretion demand). – In addition, it has been proposed that TRE may reduce fat accumulation by inducing a metabolic shift from preferential lipid synthesis and fat storage to utilization of fat when glycogen in the hepatocytes becomes depleted. – There is growing evidence in adult cohorts that eating earlier in the daytime might be more optimal for food consumption, whereas delayed eating may predispose to more metabolic dysfunction. , Several physiological features, support that an earlier start of food intake may be useful: food-induced thermogenesis is twice as high after meals in the morning as in the evening, the glucose tolerance of the body decreases continuously throughout the day, and an evening meal induces higher postprandial glucose concentrations and different secretion of insulin and incretins compared with that same meal consumed in the morning. , Thus, many adult trials have promoted TRE early in the day because it has been hypothesized to synchronize the central and peripheral circadian clocks involved in energy expenditure and fat oxidation and minimizes glycemic excursions and endogenous glucose production. , , , However, studies comparing TRE starting at different times of the day are scarce, with none to date conducted in adolescents. Many adolescents prefer to go to bed later and sleep in later, and thus an early eating window may not align with developmental and social schedules that often shift their food consumption to later in the day. – Thus, it remains unclear whether adolescents will be able to adhere to an early eating window. This shifting chronotype, coupled with increasing sex steroids and growth hormone levels produced overnight, has been shown to cause increased insulin resistance in the early morning for this age group, contrary to the physiology that is seen in adults with regards to insulin sensitivity and time of meal consumption. – Given the changing metabolic state of many adolescents living with obesity, it remains unknown how the timing of meal consumption directly effects glycemic profiles and cardiometabolic endpoints in this age group. Because of its simplicity, TRE may represent a more feasible interventional approach for adolescents with new onset T2D than other caloric restriction regimens based on macronutrient composition and kilocalories. Available preliminary data support TRE feasibility, acceptability, and safety in adolescents with obesity, without diabetes. However, no trial to date has studied the effects of TRE on glycemic control and body composition in adolescents with new onset T2D. Therefore, a 12-week, feasibility study of late TRE (lTRE; eating all food between 12:00 PM and 8:00 PM without calorie counting or recommended daily caloric intake) compared to Control (eating over a period of 12 or more hours per day) in adolescents with obesity and new onset T2D was conducted. Based on previous evidence of a preference for a later eating window in adolescents with obesity, as well as data collected in the initial pilot trial , a late eating window was selected to better align with the developmental and social schedules of adolescents in this community. We hypothesized that lTRE would be feasible in adolescents with T2D. Body weight and composition, glycemic control captured on continuous glucose monitor (CGM) and metrics of daily function (sleep, dietary intake, and physical activity) were assessed to examine the preliminary efficacy of TRE versus Control in adolescents with T2D. Based on previous TRE trials in adults with T2D, we hypothesized, that lTRE would improve hemoglobin A1c, percent time in range, weight, and body fat mass due of reduced eating time compared to Control. Moreover, we expected that reducing daily eating time would result in improved sleep quality, increase in daily physical activity, and reduction in total caloric intake compared to Control without negative effects on daily functioning. Finally, we proposed that TRE would not negatively affect eating behaviors when compared a prolonged eating window. Methods: Study Design: All participants were randomized to one of two meal-timing schedules for 12-weeks: (1) lTRE (all food consumed between 12:00 and 20:00 h (+/− 1 hour), without altering the quantity or selection of food usually consumed), or (2) Control (≥12-h eating period and 12-h fasting period during the 24 h day). Participants: The clinical trial was conducted between January 2021 and December of 2022 at Children’s Hospital Los Angeles in Los Angeles, California. Participants were recruited from clinical programs at Children’s Hospital Los Angeles and the surrounding community. Participants were eligible if they met the following criteria age 13–21 years; Tanner stage III and above; diagnosis of T2D based on the ADA diagnostic guidelines ; hemoglobin A1c ≤ 9%; metformin monotherapy; and baseline eating window greater than 10 hours. Participants were excluded if they had a diagnosis of Prader-Willi Syndrome, brain tumor or hypothalamic obesity; serious intellectual disability; previous diagnosis or subthreshold symptoms of an eating disorder (anorexia nervosa, bulimia nervosa, binge-eating disorder); parent/guardian-reported physical, mental of other inability to participate in the assessments; previous bariatric surgery; current use of weight change inducing medications (e.g., phentermine, topiramate, orlistat, glucagon-like-peptide-1 agonist, naltrexone, bupropion, SGLT-2 Inhibitor, insulin); or current participation in other interventional weight loss studies. Study procedures were approved by the Children’s Hospital Los Angeles Institutional Review Board and was in accordance with the Helsinki Declaration of 1975, as revised in 2008. The study was reported according to the Consolidated Standards of Reporting Trials (CONSORT) statement for randomized trials of nonpharmacological treatments and is registered with ClinicalTrials.gov (NCT NCT04536480 ). Written informed consent was obtained from the adolescents and one parent or guardian. Participants received compensation in the form of gift cards to complete study assessments. Randomization: Participants were randomized 1:1 to lTRE or control. The randominzation was stratified by sex and age to ensure a balanced distribution. Block size ranged from 0–6 participants. Study Assessments: The study procedures consisted of two in-person study visits (at week 0 and 12) and a virtual visit at week 4 and weekly phone calls or text check-in with the study staff. For in-person assessments, the participants visited the examination center for anthropometric measurements (body weight and composition), fasting blood tests, and questionnaires. At week 0 and 12 collection of fasting blood samples for routine laboratory tests were completed. Intervention Arms: Late Time Restricted Eating (lTRE). Participants were instructed to limit their food and beverage consumption to 8 hours from 12:00 and 20:00 (+/−1 hour) seven days per week. Participants were allowed to consume non-caloric beverages (water, tea, coffee) during the fasting period (non-caloric sweeteners were not allowed). Participants were told not to alter the quantity or selection of food usually consumed, and they were free to distribute their food and beverage

Intervention Arms: Late Time Restricted Eating (lTRE). Participants were instructed to limit their food and beverage consumption to 8 hours from 12:00 and 20:00 (+/−1 hour) seven days per week. Participants were allowed to consume non-caloric beverages (water, tea, coffee) during the fasting period (non-caloric sweeteners were not allowed). Participants were told not to alter the quantity or selection of food usually consumed, and they were free to distribute their food and beverage intake into meals and snacks over the 8-hour window. Control. Participants in the prolonged eating window were instructed to consume their foods and beverages over a 12-hour or more eating window seven days per week. Participants were asked not to alter the quantity or selection of food usually consumed, and they were free to distribute their food and beverage intake into meals and snacks over the +12-hour window. Procedures common to both study arms. All participants received two hours of standard nutrition counseling recommended for adolescents living with T2D delivered by the clinical dietetic program at Children’s Hospital Los Angeles as part of standard new onset education curriculum. No specific caloric restriction was recommended. All participants were trained to wear a continuous glucose monitor (CGM) sensor using manufacturer educational materials under the supervision of research staff. Participants were asked to wear the CGM for the duration of the study. All participants wore unblinded, Dexcom G6 CGM (Dexcom, San Diego, CA, USA) continuously during the study period. Participants were provided with a transmitter and enough sensors to replace the sensor every 10 days. The participants and guardians were educated on how to use the CGM and received 1:1 coaching on how to change the sensor, which was completed either independently or under study team guidance. No glucometer calibration was required. At each weekly phone meeting, study staff monitored any adverse events and challenges related to CGM wear, including participant discomfort, skin adherence, and other issues. Adherence monitoring. The study staff performed weekly phone or text encounters with the participants to assess barriers to adherence including diabetes specific components and eating practices (responding to hunger cues, managing fasting periods in social situations, etc.). If a barrier was identified the study staff created a solution plan to promote adherence, and retention. The study staff recorded any medication changes or health issues that occurred in the last 7 days. All participants recorded the time they started and finished eating daily and provided their eating logs to the study staff weekly. These self-reported time windows were verified by examining the pattern of glucose excursions using the 24-h CGM data. If a glucose excursion of greater than 80 mg/dL was identified the report fasting period, the occasion was reviewed with the participant to verify if an eating event occurred during the self-reported fasting period. If a participant didn’t adhere to meal timing protocol at least 4 days/week, a follow-up call or videoconference was scheduled to address challenges, give participants additional encouragement, support, and a personalized plan to promote adherence was created. Measurements: The primary endpoint of the study was feasibility. Feasibility was operationalized by recruitment rate, retention rate, the number of days adolescents complied with their prescribed eating window, and satisfaction with lTRE. Satisfaction was captured via questionnaire and semi-structured interviews. The interviews with the participants were conducted using a semi-structured interview guide developed by the study team that included qualitative open-ended questions and quantitative close-ended questions. The qualitative questions were asked at the beginning of the interview to document factors not previously considered or known. These questions asked participants to describe what they liked and disliked about the treatment arm they were randomized to, including various aspects of the intervention and the study’s assessment activities. The participants were also asked to describe what changes, if any, they would like to see implemented if they were selected again as participants in a TRE focused trial for youth. The qualitative open-ended questions were intentionally broad to make the topics as accessible as possible. Interviewers made written notes of short-hand quotations as the interview progressed and then added to these notes and expanded quotations once the interview was completed. Participants were also encouraged to respond freely to a set of quantitative closed-ended questions that aimed to evaluate participant views on acceptability of the interventions and study assessments. Six questions were asked about acceptability, in terms of likability, perceived helpfulness, ease of use, and referral of the interventions to others. Physical Activity: Physical activity was assessed using the Patient Reported Outcomes Measurement Information System (PROMIS ® ) . The PROMIS ® instruments were developed using rigorous qualitative and quantitative methods and standardized to a reference population. The PROMIS ® measures for children have been found to demonstrate feasibility, internal consistency, construct validity, and responsiveness to change in a clinical setting. The physical activity survey is a self-administered 7-day recall instrument developed to assess the general levels of physical activity of children and adolescents. A score of 50 is the average for the United States general population with a standard error of 10 because calibration testing was performed on a large sample of the general population. The T-score is provided with an error term (Standard Error or SE). A higher PROMIS T-score represents more of the concept being measured (i.e., physical activity). Dietary Intake: The 24-hour dietary recalls were collected using Nutrition Data System for Research (NDSR) for Research software version 2015 (May 2015), a computer-based software application developed at the University of Minnesota Nutrition Coordinating Center (NCC) that facilitates the collection of recalls in a standardized manner. Dietary intake data was gathered via semi-structured interview, conducted either in-person or virtually with the participant, via a multiple-pass interview approach. The first pass involved obtaining from the participant a listing of all foods and beverages consumed in the previous 24 hours. This information was then reviewed with the participant. The interviewer then collected detailed information about each reported food and beverage. The interviewer then probed for commonly forgotten foods. Finally, the detailed information was reviewed for completeness and correctness. , Two 24-hour dietary recalls (one weekday and one weekend day) were analyzed for each participant at two study time points: baseline and week 12. The 24-hour recalls were analyzed for total energy intake and macronutrient composition. The mean total energy intake and macronutrient composition for both 24-hour recalls were analyzed at each time point. The reported timing of food intake was used to monitor participant adherence to the designated eating window. Sleep: The Pittsburg Sleep Quality Index (PSQI) was collected at baseline and week 12. The PSQI evaluates seven components of sleep architecture, sleep quality, sleep latency, sleep duration, habitual sleep efficiency, sleep disturbances, use of sleeping medication, and daytime dysfunction and is widely used in research and clinical settings as a measure of sleep quality. , – The PSQI is a self-rated questionnaire that assesses sleep quality over the course of a one-month period. The individual 19 items in PSQI are aggregated into seven components that assess various aspects of sleep, and the sum of these seven components yields a global score that discriminates between “good” and “poor” sleepers. The questionnaire has been widely validated and used in both non-clinical and clinical samples, and across different age groups, having been translated into and validated for different languages. The PSQI score is calculated from seven components of sleep quality (derived from 19 individual items) that are rated from 0 to 3, yielding a global score ranging from 0 to 21, where the higher score indicates worse sleep. The seven components of sleep quality include measures of subjective sleep quality, sleep onset latency, sleep duration, habitual sleep efficiency, sleep disturbances, use of sleeping medications and daytime dysfunction. A score of 7 or higher indicates poor sleep quality. The original PSQI had an internal consistency of 0.83. Statistical Analysis The study was a feasibility trial; thus, a convenient sample size was used to estimate parameters for a larger, fully powered trial. NDSR, PROMIS ® PA, and BEDS questionnaires were summarized according to prior literature. Adherence was operationalized as the number of days adolescents complied with their prescribed eating window, number of weekly phone calls and scheduled research visits they attended, and satisfaction scores. Baseline demographics and characteristics were summarized descriptively across arms using mean and standard deviation (SD) or median and interquartile range as appropriate for the distribution of continuous variables. Categorical variables are described as a frequency and percentage. The differences in demographics, anthropometrics baseline, and eating window distributions among intervention groups were examined using Wilcoxon rank sum test and Fisher’s exact test. To assess whether there were between-group differences in mean change (from baseline) in clinical outcomes at Week 12, mixed-effects longitudinal regression models (lmerTest package in RStudio) with fixed study arm, study visit, study arm*study visit, and baseline outcome values as well as covariates (baseline HbA1c, baseline %BMI p95 , and sex) were used. Models included random intercepts to account for within-subject correlation between repeated outcomes over time. Analyses were based on the intention to treat (ITT) population, whereby all participants with data at baseline were included in analyses according to arm to which they were randomized, regardless of adherence to the study protocol (n= 27). Mixed-effects analyses are generally robust for unbalanced data across study time points where information from the observed data is used to provide information about the missing data without explicitly imputing the missing outcome values using the likelihood-based approach. All results were reported with 95% confidence interval and p -value. The statistical significance level was set at .05 with two-sided throughout the analyses. All statistical computations were done in RStudio 4.2.2. There were no reports of headache, dizziness, fatigue, halitosis, dry mouth, nausea, or constipation in either the lTRE or Control group. Four participants of the initial 27, had positive BEDS-7 scores (answered yes to having episodes of excessive overeating over the past 3-month) at baseline (1: lTRE and 3: Control), at week 12 for these four participants all BED-S-7 scores were negative. For the 23 participants with negative BEDS-7 scores (answered no to having episodes of excessive overeating over the past 3-month) at baseline, only one participant reported a positive BEDS-7 score over the study period from the Control group. All participant with positive BEDS-7 scores went on to receive full evaluation for disordered eating by a trained professional and none met criteria for a diagnosis. Discussion: To our knowledge, this is the first study to examine the feasibility of late eight-hour TRE in adolescents with type 2 diabetes. The results demonstrate that 1) late 8-hour TRE is feasible, safe, and acceptable in this cohort; 2) for a subset of participants lTRE can result in clinically meaningful weight loss and reduction in alanine transaminase; 3) lTRE resulted in a significant caloric reduction with a decrease in total added sugar and carbohydrates consumed, when compared to control; and 4) lTRE did not negatively impact sleep, eating behaviors, or physical activity. Neither lTRE nor Control were associated with changes in glycemic control, total body fat mass, or cholesterol levels. These findings suggest that lTRE may be used as an alternative dietary approach in adolescents with T2D. Onset of a type 2 diabetes diagnosis in adolescents has been reported as a challenging time for recruitment into clinical trials. Despite these findings, recruitment and adherences rates were quite high. Adherence to TRE was high, with participants adhering to the late 8-hour eating window on average 6 out of 7 days per week over the 12-week study period. This finding is consistent with a previous pilot study, conducted by Vidmar et al ., of late 8-hour TRE in adolescents with obesity, without diabetes, further highlighting the feasibility of this approach in this age group. In comparison, caloric restriction interventions, in this age group frequently have adherence rates of as low as 50%, even for short term intervention periods. – TRE does not require adolescents to alter their home eating environment completely and thus allows both more autonomy and higher likelihood of whole family engagement and sustained involvement. While this study was not powered to measure the effects of lTRE on clinical outcomes it provides insight into how TRE effects cardiometabolic risk factors in adolescents with T2D. As expected, there was a great heterogeneity in weight responses to this intervention with no significant difference between lTRE and Control over the study period. For a subset of participants (6/13), lTRE did result in clinically meaningful weight loss of more than 5% weight loss at week 12 compared to baseline. Interestingly, there was not a significant association between the degree of weight reduction and lTRE adherence. The average degree of energy restriction achieved with late 8-hour TRE was comparable to that of what has been reported in many studies of energy restriction and TRE studies in adult cohorts. , , Based on previous work conducted by Vidmar et al. an afternoon/evening eating window was selected to align with adolescent preferences. However, it remains unknown if the timing of the eating window may affect the clinical outcomes of TRE. Chow et al. conducted a 12-week study of 8-hour TRE without caloric restriction compared to a no-treatment control in adults with obesity and showed that TRE resulted in a 4% weight loss compared to control and that the degree of weight loss was associated with the degree of restriction of the eating

energy restriction and TRE studies in adult cohorts. , , Based on previous work conducted by Vidmar et al. an afternoon/evening eating window was selected to align with adolescent preferences. However, it remains unknown if the timing of the eating window may affect the clinical outcomes of TRE. Chow et al. conducted a 12-week study of 8-hour TRE without caloric restriction compared to a no-treatment control in adults with obesity and showed that TRE resulted in a 4% weight loss compared to control and that the degree of weight loss was associated with the degree of restriction of the eating window. – This is important to consider in the present study as, in contrast to adult data, the baseline eating window for this pediatric cohort was quite restricted. Thus, the lack of observed difference between groups may have been due to a modest reduction in eating window given participants were starting at a baseline of 10 hours versus 14 to 15 hours as reported in many adult studies. These findings emphasize the importance of better understanding how shifting chronobiology impacts eating windows and timing in adolescents with obesity and T2D to determine the best execution of time-based approaches in this age group. , , Interestingly, in this cohort despite not requiring participants to count calories or adjust diet quality, lTRE resulted in a statistically significant reduction in energy intake of 271 calories/day compared to an increase in Control. This finding has been reported in adult cohorts under TRE conditions without intentional caloric restriction highlighting that limiting the eating window often results in a natural reduction in daily caloric intake. , , Despite thoughtful, patient-centered, delivery of standard nutrition recommendations for youth onset type 2 diabetes many adolescents living with T2D are unable to consistently adhere to these recommendations consistently limiting their efficacy and sustainability. , Berkowitz et al. reported common barriers to standard medical nutrition approaches for adolescents include lack of access to fresh foods, additional cost, challenges with frequent logging, and ability to change the home food environment. TRE may be a more simplistic, developmentally appropriate nutrition approach for some adolescents and add to the available of options to these adolescents as part of their medical regimen. TRE may be more easily implemented across historically marginalized communities in which the rates of diabetes onset in adolescents are the greatest compared to dietary approaches that require high cost and significant change to the home food environment. Limitations This study has several limitations. First, the sample size was small, and was underpowered to detect differences between groups for certain secondary outcome measures including weight reduction, change in hemoglobin A1c, and ALT. A larger clinical trial, over a longer duration and powered for these secondary outcomes is warranted. The short study duration may have affected the study outcomes. In this cohort, a sub-group of the control arm also showed a significant reduction in %BMI p95 and therefore a longer study duration would provide further information regarding whether this finding would sustain overtime in the no-treatment arm. Second, a more robust crossover design was considered. A cross-over trial could help to reduce the influence of confounding covariates, as each participant would act as their own control. However, given the behavioral components of the approach, there was a high risk of contamination and bias that would be unable to be separated appropriately between TRE and control in this age group. Third, the effects of the 8-h regimen at different times in the day (early versus late) was not evaluated. An alternative intervention design that prescribed an early eating window to align with mechanistic data that suggests early eating may be more effective for improving cardiometabolic endpoints in TRE trials in adults was considered. , , However, based on preliminary studies, an early eating window would conflict with the average social eating schedule of many adolescents. Thus, the feasibility of an afternoon/evening eating period was examined to promote sustained adherence and engagement. It is possible that if the eating window were shifted to earlier in the day, more pronounced reductions in insulin resistance would have been noted. Given that there were high responders in both the lTRE and Control arm there may have been intervention components across both intervention arms that contributed to meaningful weight reduction. One such component may have been the unblinded CGM. While there is limited data on the whether CGM use in youth with T2D effects weight trajectory there is growing interest in utilizing wearable technology to promote weight loss across the lifespan. – In addition, unblinded CGMs have been utilized in adult cohorts as a behavioral modification tool to promote sustained change to nutrition based on post prandial glycemic excursions. This type of pattern recognition was not taught to participants in this cohort specifically, however may have had an unmeasurable

components across both intervention arms that contributed to meaningful weight reduction. One such component may have been the unblinded CGM. While there is limited data on the whether CGM use in youth with T2D effects weight trajectory there is growing interest in utilizing wearable technology to promote weight loss across the lifespan. – In addition, unblinded CGMs have been utilized in adult cohorts as a behavioral modification tool to promote sustained change to nutrition based on post prandial glycemic excursions. This type of pattern recognition was not taught to participants in this cohort specifically, however may have had an unmeasurable effect that was not controlled for. Conclusions Data from this study indicate adolescents with T2D can be recruited and retained to participate in a lTRE intervention and decreasing their eating window is acceptable. During a 12-week period, TRE 6 days/week is feasible for adolescents with T2D. These preliminary data provide strong support for further investigations into the effect of TRE on weight and glycemic control in adolescents with T2D. Future longer term studies are needed to investigate the efficacy of TRE in adolescents with T2D, discover the optimal timing of the eating window, elucidate the mechanism of action of TRE, and find the best methods to administer TRE across all communities.
